summaries.summary: Data imbalance affects NLP tagging and MRC tasks, with class O ratios of 5 on CoNLL03, 8 on OntoNotes5.0, and negative-positive ratios of 50-200.
Data imbalance causes training-test discrepancy and easy-negative overwhelming, while CE or MLE objectives handle neither issue.
The authors propose replacing CE or MLE with Sørensen–Dice coefficient or Tversky index losses to address the first issue.
A dynamic weight adjusting strategy using weights proportional to (1-p) deemphasizes confident examples and alleviates easy-negative domination.

Combined strategies yield SOTA POS results on CTB5 (97.92, +1.86), CTB6 (96.57, +1.80), UD1.4 (96.98, +2.19), and SOTA NER results on CoNLL03 (93.33, +0.29), OntoNotes5.0 (92.07, +0.96)), MSRA 96.72(+0.97), and OntoNotes4.0 (84.47,+2.36).
The paper presents related work in Section 2, training objectives in Section 3, experiments in Section 4, ablation studies in Section 5, and conclusion in Section 6.
Prior weighting and resampling methods include importance sampling, AdaBoost, hard example mining, oversampling, focal loss, self-paced learning, loss-based adjustment, and learned sample weights.
Object detection work on background-object imbalance, including HNM, OHEM, 3:1 negative-positive sampling, IoU-balanced sampling, and average-precision loss, inspired the NLP approach.
Binary classification illustrates how different losses work, with the mechanism easily extended to multi-class classification.
Instances x_i have golden label vectors y_i = [y_{i0},y_{i1}] and probability vectors p_i = [p_{i0},p_{i1}] for negative and positive labels.
The vanilla cross entropy (CE) loss is given.
In CE, each x_i contributes equally, while class weighting factor α or dataset resampling can treat examples unequally.
The coefficient α is calculated using lg((n-n_t)/n_t+K), with K tuned, while weighting and resampling are equivalent but rarely used due to tricky α selection.
Sørensen–Dice coefficient, dice coefficient (DSC), is an F1-oriented statistic measuring similarity of two sets A and B.
A contains all positive examples predicted by a model, B contains all golden positive examples, and DSC is written using TP, FP, and FN.
For an individual example x_i, its corresponding DSC loss is given.
A negative example with y_{i1}=0 does not contribute, so a γ factor is commonly added to numerator and denominator for smoothing.
With γ, negative examples contribute with DSC γ/(p_{i1}+γ), and milletari2016v proposed a squared denominator for faster convergence, yielding dice loss (DL).
Another DL version computes set-level dice coefficient, but the authors choose the sum of individual dice coefficient for ease of optimization.
Tversky index (TI), an approximation of the F_{β} score, extends dice coefficient to a more general case for sets A and B.
Tversky index controls false-negative and false-positive tradeoff, degenerates to DSC if α=β=0.5, and defines Tversky loss (TL) for {x_i,y_i}.
For one example x_i classified positive when p_{i1} exceeds 0.5, the F1 score computation is shown.
Eq.DISPLAY_FORM14 is a soft F1 using continuous p rather than binary I(p_{i1}>0.5), which is detrimental with many easy-negative examples.
The authors multiply soft probability p by decaying factor (1-p), changing Eq.DISPLAY_FORM22.
The weight (1-p_{i1}) changes during training, and (1-p_{i1})p_{i1} reduces focus on easy examples as probabilities approach 0 or 1.
Eq.DISPLAY_FORM14 mimics focal loss (FL), which down-weights well-classified examples using (1-p)^{β} and yields (1-p)^{β}log p.

The method is evaluated on part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, machine reading comprehension, and paraphrase identification, with baselines optimized by standard cross-entropy.
POS assigns labels to words; the paper uses BERT on three Chinese POS datasets and reports span-level micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1.
Experiments use Chinese Treebank 5.0, 6.0, and UD1.4.
CTB5 is a Chinese tagging and parsing dataset with 507,222 words, 824,983 characters, and 18,782 sentences from newswire sources.
CTB6 extends CTB5 and contains 781,351 words, 1,285,149 characters, and 28,295 sentences.
UD abbreviates Universal Dependencies, a framework for consistent grammar annotation, and this work uses UD1.4 for Chinese POS tagging.
The following baselines are used.
Joint-POS from shao2017character jointly learns Chinese word segmentation and POS.
Lattice-LSTM from lattice2018zhang constructs a word-character lattice.
Bert-Tagger from devlin2018bert treats part-of-speech as a tagging task.
DSC loss outperforms BERT-tagger by +1.86 F1 on CTB5, +1.80 on CTB6, and +2.19 on UD1.4, achieving SOTA robustly.

NER detects entity spans and categories; the implementation uses BERT-MRC, BERT_Large English checkpoints, official Chinese checkpoints, and reports span-level micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score.
NER datasets include Chinese OntoNotes4.0 and MSRA and English CoNLL2003 and OntoNotes5.0.
CoNLL2003 is an English dataset with 4 entity types: Location, Organization, Person, and Miscellaneous, following BIBREF14 processing protocols.
English OntoNotes5.0 contains texts from varied sources and 18 entity types, using the standard CoNLL2012 shared task train/dev/test split.
Chinese MSRA is a news-domain benchmark with 3 entity types, uses a 9:1 training-development split, and uses the official test set.
Chinese OntoNotes4.0 is a Chinese news-domain dataset with 18 entity types, using the same data split as wu2019glyce.
ELMo is a tagging model from peters2018deep.
Lattice-LSTM from lattice2018zhang constructs a word-character lattice and is only used in Chinese datasets.
CVT from kevin2018cross uses Cross-View Training(CVT) to improve representations of a Bi-LSTM encoder.
Bert-Tagger from devlin2018bert treats NER as a tagging task.
Glyce-BERT from wu2019glyce combines glyph information with BERT pretraining.
BERT-MRC from xiaoya2019ner is the current SOTA model for Chinese and English NER datasets and formulates NER as machine reading comprehension.
The proposed method outperforms BERT-MRCBIBREF38 by +0.29 on CoNLL2003 and +0.96 on OntoNotes5.0, and improves F1 by +0.97 on MSRA and +2.36 on OntoNotes4.0.
MRC is central to natural language understanding; the paper uses SQuAD-style answer span prediction and reports Extract Match (EM) and F1 score on validation set.
Five MRC datasets are used: SQuAD v1.1, SQuAD v2.0 BIBREF4, BIBREF6, and Quoref BIBREF8.
SQuAD v1.1 and SQuAD v2.0 are widely used QA benchmarks; SQuAD1.1 has 100K crowdsourced question-answer pairs, and SQuAD2.0 allows no short answer.
Quoref tests coreferential reasoning in reading comprehension systems and contains 24K questions over 4.7K paragraphs from Wikipedia.
QANet builds a model based on convolutions and self-attention, with convolution modeling local interactions and self-attention modeling global interactions.
BERT treats NER as a tagging task.
XLNet proposes a generalized autoregressive pretraining method that enables learning bidirectional contexts.
DSC loss significantly boosts EM and F1 with BERT or XLNet on MRC tasks, outperforming XLNet on SQuADv1.1, SQuAD v2.0, and QuoRef.
Paraphrase identification identifies whether two sentences have the same meaning, using BERT and XLNet backbones and reporting F1 score.
Experiments for PI task are conducted on two widely used datasets: MRPC and QQP.
MRPC contains automatically extracted online news sentence pairs with human semantic-equivalence annotations and imbalanced classes of 68% positive and 32% negative.
QQP is a collection of Quora question pairs with an unbalanced class distribution of 37% positive and 63% negative.
Replacing the training objective with DSC boosts BERT and XLNet, improving F1 by +0.58 for MRPC and +0.73 for QQP.
Experiments on SST-2 and SST-5 show DL and DSC slightly reduce accuracy compared with CE, indicating dice loss works well for F1 but not accuracy.
Tversky index hyperparameters α and β affect precision-recall tradeoff, with highest F1 of 84.67 on Chinese OntoNotes4.0 at α 0.6 and 68.44 on QuoRef at α 0.4.
The paper proposes dice loss to replace cross-entropy for data-imbalanced NLP tasks, narrowing objective-metric gaps and boosting part-of-speech, NER, MRC, and PI tasks.
